name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q01 - Driving force for chemical bond formation

questiontext.text: Why do atoms of most elements combine to form molecules rather than existing as independent atoms under normal conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Every physical and chemical system naturally tends toward a state of greater stability, which corresponds to minimum potential energy.

Step 2: Evaluation
Chemical bonding is nature's way of lowering the total energy of the system of combining atoms so that the resulting molecule is more stable than the isolated atoms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Atoms combine to lower the energy of the system and attain stability.

answer.text: To lower the energy of the system and attain stability
To increase the potential energy of the valence electrons
To eliminate all electrostatic interactions between nuclei and electrons
To convert inner-shell electrons into valence electrons

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q02 - Significance of Lewis symbols and group valence

questiontext.text: What do the dots around the symbol of an element in a Lewis symbol represent, and how is its group valence generally related to this number?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In chemical combination, only the outer-shell (valence) electrons participate, while inner-shell electrons are well protected.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a Lewis symbol, the number of dots around the atomic symbol represents the number of valence electrons. The common or group valence of the element is generally equal either to the number of dots or to \(8\) minus the number of dots.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The dots represent valence electrons, and the group valence is equal to the number of dots or \(8 - \text{number of dots}\).

answer.text: Total electrons; group valence equals \(8 + \text{number of dots}\)
Valence electrons; group valence equals the number of dots or \(8 - \text{number of dots}\)
Inner-shell electrons; group valence equals \(2 \times \text{number of dots}\)
Unpaired \(p\)-electrons only; group valence equals \(4 - \text{number of dots}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q03 - Electrovalence of calcium and fluorine in CaF2

questiontext.text: In the formation of \(\mathrm{CaF}_{2}\) according to Kössel's approach, what are the electrovalences assigned to calcium and fluorine, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrovalence is equal to the number of unit charge(s) on the ion formed by electron transfer.

Step 2: Evaluation
Calcium (\([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^{2}\)) loses two electrons to form \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), attaining a positive electrovalence of \(+2\). Fluorine (\([\mathrm{He}]2s^{2}2p^{5}\)) gains one electron to form \(\mathrm{F}^{-}\), attaining a negative electrovalence of \(-1\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Calcium has an electrovalence of \(+2\) and fluorine has an electrovalence of \(-1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q04 - Langmuir covalent bond concept in Cl2

questiontext.text: Who refined the Lewis postulations by abandoning the idea of a stationary cubical arrangement of the octet and introducing the term "covalent bond"?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In 1919, Langmuir modified Lewis's cubical atom model to describe bonding through shared electron pairs.

Step 2: Evaluation
Langmuir abandoned the stationary cubical octet picture and introduced the term "covalent bond" to explain molecules such as \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\), where each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Langmuir introduced the term covalent bond.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q05 - Shared electron pairs in dinitrogen molecule

questiontext.text: How many electron pairs are shared between the two nitrogen atoms in a \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) molecule to achieve an octet configuration?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each nitrogen atom has \(5\) valence electrons and requires \(3\) more electrons to complete its octet.

Step 2: Evaluation
To attain the octet, the two nitrogen atoms share \(3\) electron pairs (\(6\) electrons) between them, forming a triple covalent bond (\(\mathrm{N}\equiv\mathrm{N}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Three electron pairs are shared between the two nitrogen atoms in \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q06 - Definition of lattice enthalpy

questiontext.text: The lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid is defined as the energy required to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lattice enthalpy measures the strength of electrostatic interactions holding a three-dimensional ionic crystal together.

Step 2: Evaluation
It is defined as the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous constituent ions at an infinite distance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lattice enthalpy is the energy needed to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into gaseous constituent ions.

answer.text: Convert one mole of gaseous atoms into gaseous ions
Completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into gaseous constituent ions
Break one mole of covalent bonds in the gaseous state
Melt one mole of a solid ionic compound into its liquid state

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q07 - Covalent radius versus van der Waals radius in chlorine

questiontext.text: For a chlorine molecule (\(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\)) in the solid state, how does the covalent radius (\(r_{\mathrm{cov}}\)) compare with the van der Waals radius (\(r_{\mathrm{vdw}}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Covalent radius is half the distance between two similar atoms joined by a covalent bond in the same molecule, whereas van der Waals radius is half the distance between two similar atoms in separate adjacent molecules.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because bonded atoms undergo orbital overlap and are held closely together, the internuclear distance within \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\) (\(198\ \mathrm{pm}\), giving \(r_{\mathrm{cov}} = 99\ \mathrm{pm}\)) is much smaller than the nonbonded distance between adjacent \(\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\) molecules (\(360\ \mathrm{pm}\), giving \(r_{\mathrm{vdw}} = 180\ \mathrm{pm}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The covalent radius is smaller than the van der Waals radius (\(r_{\mathrm{cov}} < r_{\mathrm{vdw}}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q08 - Conversion between Debye and SI units of dipole moment

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly expresses \(1\ \mathrm{Debye}\ (\mathrm{D})\) in SI units (\(\mathrm{C\ m}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dipole moment (\(\mu = Q \times r\)) is commonly expressed in Debye units (\(\mathrm{D}\)) and has SI units of coulomb-metre (\(\mathrm{C\ m}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
The standard conversion factor between Debye and \(\mathrm{C\ m}\) is \(1\ \mathrm{D} = 3.33564 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(1\ \mathrm{D} = 3.33564 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q09 - VSEPR geometry of BF3 molecule

questiontext.text: According to VSEPR theory, what are the molecular geometry and bond angle of \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\), the central boron atom has \(3\) bonding electron pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(\mathrm{AB}_{3}\) type).

Step 2: Evaluation
To minimize repulsion, the three electron pairs arrange themselves in a plane at maximum separation, resulting in a trigonal planar geometry with \(\mathrm{F-B-F}\) bond angles of \(120^{\circ}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) has a trigonal planar geometry with a bond angle of \(120^{\circ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q10 - Mode of orbital overlap in sigma and pi bonds

questiontext.text: In valence bond theory, how are a sigma (\(\sigma\)) bond and a pi (\(\pi\)) bond formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Covalent bonds are classified as \(\sigma\) or \(\pi\) depending on the orientation of the overlapping atomic orbitals relative to the internuclear axis.

Step 2: Evaluation
A \(\sigma\) bond is formed by end-to-end (head-on/axial) overlap of bonding orbitals along the internuclear axis, whereas a \(\pi\) bond is formed by sidewise (lateral) overlap of orbitals whose axes remain parallel to each other and perpendicular to the internuclear axis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A \(\sigma\) bond forms by head-on axial overlap, and a \(\pi\) bond forms by sidewise overlap perpendicular to the internuclear axis.

answer.text: \(\sigma\) bond by sidewise overlap; \(\pi\) bond by axial overlap
\(\sigma\) bond by head-on axial overlap; \(\pi\) bond by sidewise overlap
Both \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) bonds by head-on axial overlap

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q11 - Percentage s-character in sp3 and sp hybrid orbitals

questiontext.text: What is the percentage of \(s\)-character in an \(sp\) hybrid orbital and an \(sp^{3}\) hybrid orbital, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The percentage of \(s\)-character in a hybrid orbital equals the fraction of \(s\)-orbital contribution multiplied by \(100\).

Step 2: Evaluation
An \(sp\) hybrid orbital is formed from \(1\) \(s\) and \(1\) \(p\) orbital (\(2\) orbitals total), giving \(\frac{1}{2} \times 100 = 50\%\) \(s\)-character. An \(sp^{3}\) hybrid orbital is formed from \(1\) \(s\) and \(3\) \(p\) orbitals (\(4\) orbitals total), giving \(\frac{1}{4} \times 100 = 25\%\) \(s\)-character.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(s\)-character is \(50\%\) for \(sp\) and \(25\%\) for \(sp^{3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q12 - Electronegative elements forming hydrogen bonds

questiontext.text: Hydrogen bonding is typically formed when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to which set of highly electronegative elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A hydrogen bond is the attractive force that binds a partially positively charged hydrogen atom (\(\mathrm{H}^{\delta+}\)) of one molecule with a strongly electronegative atom of another molecule (or within the same molecule).

Step 2: Evaluation
Only the highly electronegative elements fluorine (\(\mathrm{F}\)), oxygen (\(\mathrm{O}\)), and nitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}\)) withdraw sufficient electron density from hydrogen to produce strong hydrogen bonding.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hydrogen bonding occurs with \(\mathrm{F}\), \(\mathrm{O}\), and \(\mathrm{N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q13 - Lewis structure of carbon monoxide

questiontext.text: In the Lewis dot structure of the \(\mathrm{CO}\) molecule that satisfies the octet rule for both atoms, how many bonding electron pairs and lone pairs are present?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Carbon has valence shell configuration \(2s^{2}2p^{2}\) (\(4\) valence electrons) and oxygen has \(2s^{2}2p^{4}\) (\(6\) valence electrons).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Total available valence electrons \(= 4 + 6 = 10\) electrons (\(5\) pairs). Both \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\) must attain an octet.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Each covalent bond uses \(1\) shared pair of electrons.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
To satisfy the octet on both carbon and oxygen using \(10\) electrons, a triple bond (\(\mathrm{:C\equiv O:}\)) is formed between \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\). This accounts for \(3\) shared bonding pairs (\(6\) electrons), leaving \(4\) electrons as \(1\) lone pair on carbon and \(1\) lone pair on oxygen (\(2\) lone pairs total).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Carbon has \(6 + 2 = 8\) electrons and oxygen has \(6 + 2 = 8\) electrons. Thus, there are \(3\) bonding pairs and \(2\) lone pairs.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q14 - Formal charges on oxygen atoms in ozone

questiontext.text: In the Lewis structure of ozone (\(\mathrm{O}_{3}\)), where the central oxygen atom forms one double bond and one single bond with the two terminal oxygen atoms, what are the formal charges on the central, double-bonded terminal, and single-bonded terminal oxygen atoms, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Each free oxygen atom has \(V = 6\) valence electrons. In the \(\mathrm{O}_{3}\) Lewis structure, the central \(\mathrm{O}\) has \(1\) lone pair (\(L = 2\)) and \(3\) bonds (\(B = 6\)); the double-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\) has \(2\) lone pairs (\(L = 4\)) and \(2\) bonds (\(B = 4\)); the single-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\) has \(3\) lone pairs (\(L = 6\)) and \(1\) bond (\(B = 2\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Formal charge assumes equal sharing of bonding electrons between adjacent atoms.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\mathrm{F.C.} = V - L - \frac{1}{2}B\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Central \(\mathrm{O}\): \(6 - 2 - \frac{1}{2}(6) = +1\).
- Double-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\): \(6 - 4 - \frac{1}{2}(4) = 0\).
- Single-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\): \(6 - 6 - \frac{1}{2}(2) = -1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Sum of formal charges \(= +1 + 0 + (-1) = 0\), matching a neutral \(\mathrm{O}_{3}\) molecule. The formal charges are \(+1,\ 0,\ -1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q15 - Incomplete octet exception examples

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of molecules consists exclusively of compounds with an incomplete octet around the central atom?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Compounds of elements having fewer than four valence electrons (such as \(\mathrm{Li}\), \(\mathrm{Be}\), \(\mathrm{B}\), and \(\mathrm{Al}\)) often have fewer than \(8\) electrons around the central atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{LiCl}\), \(\mathrm{BeH}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{BCl}_{3}\), and \(\mathrm{AlCl}_{3}\), the central atoms have \(2\), \(4\), \(6\), and \(6\) valence electrons around them, respectively—all less than \(8\). By contrast, \(\mathrm{PF}_{5}\) and \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\) have expanded octets (\(10\) and \(12\) electrons), \(\mathrm{NO}\) is an odd-electron molecule, and \(\mathrm{CCl}_{4}\) obeys the octet rule.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{LiCl}\), \(\mathrm{BeH}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{BCl}_{3}\), and \(\mathrm{AlCl}_{3}\) all have an incomplete octet.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q16 - Expanded octet and odd-electron exceptions

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of an odd-electron molecule in which the octet rule is not satisfied for all atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecules with an odd total number of valence electrons cannot pair all electrons to give every atom an octet.

Step 2: Evaluation
Nitric oxide (\(\mathrm{NO}\)) has \(5 + 6 = 11\) valence electrons, making it an odd-electron molecule. \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{SCl}_{2}\) all have even numbers of valence electrons and satisfy the octet rule.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{NO}\) is an odd-electron molecule that does not satisfy the octet rule.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q17 - Sulphur compound obeying the octet rule

questiontext.text: Although sulphur forms several compounds with an expanded octet, in which of the following compounds does the central sulphur atom strictly obey the octet rule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sulphur has \(6\) valence electrons; if it forms \(2\) single covalent bonds and retains \(2\) lone pairs, it has \(8\) electrons in its valence shell.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{SCl}_{2}\), sulphur shares two electron pairs with two \(\mathrm{Cl}\) atoms and has two lone pairs, giving \(8\) electrons around \(\mathrm{S}\) (octet obeyed). In \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\), sulphur has \(12\) valence electrons (expanded octet), and in \(\mathrm{SF}_{4}\) it has \(10\) valence electrons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The central sulphur atom obeys the octet rule in \(\mathrm{SCl}_{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q19 - Non-metallic cation exception in ionic compounds

questiontext.text: Most ionic compounds have cations derived from metallic elements. Which of the following is an exception that forms the cation of a number of ionic compounds despite being composed entirely of non-metallic elements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionic solids typically consist of metallic cations and non-metallic anions, though certain polyatomic cations formed from non-metals can also form ionic lattices.

Step 2: Evaluation
The ammonium ion (\(\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}\)) is composed of two non-metallic elements (nitrogen and hydrogen) yet acts as a stable cation in many ionic compounds (such as \(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\mathrm{Cl}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q20 - Mean O-H bond enthalpy in water

questiontext.text: For \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})\), the stepwise bond dissociation enthalpies are \(\Delta_{a}H_{1}^{\circ} = 502\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{OH}(\mathrm{g})\) and \(\Delta_{a}H_{2}^{\circ} = 427\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for \(\mathrm{OH}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})\). What is the mean \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond enthalpy in water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\Delta_{a}H_{1}^{\circ} = 502\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), \(\Delta_{a}H_{2}^{\circ} = 427\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), and number of \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bonds broken \(= 2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Bond dissociation enthalpies are positive (endothermic) quantities.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\text{Average bond enthalpy} = \frac{\Delta_{a}H_{1}^{\circ} + \Delta_{a}H_{2}^{\circ}}{2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\text{Average bond enthalpy} = \frac{502 + 427}{2} = \frac{929}{2} = 464.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The average value lies midway between \(427\) and \(502\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). The mean \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond enthalpy is \(464.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q21 - Isoelectronic species with identical bond order

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups of molecules/ions are isoelectronic and possess an identical bond order of \(3\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isoelectronic molecules and ions have the same total number of electrons and therefore identical bond orders.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) (\(7 + 7 = 14\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)), \(\mathrm{CO}\) (\(6 + 8 = 14\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)), and \(\mathrm{NO}^{+}\) (\(7 + 8 - 1 = 14\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)) are all \(14\)-electron isoelectronic species with a bond order of \(3\). By contrast, \(\mathrm{F}_{2}\) and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\) have \(18\) electrons (bond order \(1\)), and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) has \(16\) electrons (bond order \(2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{N}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{CO}\), and \(\mathrm{NO}^{+}\) are isoelectronic with bond order \(3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q22 - Resonance averaging of bond lengths in ozone

generalfeedback.text:

Resonance averages the bond characteristics of all canonical forms, making equivalent bonds identical in length and intermediate between single and double bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{O}_{3}\), both oxygen–oxygen bonds in the resonance hybrid are experimentally found to be equal at \(128\ \mathrm{pm}\), which lies between \(121\ \mathrm{pm}\) and \(148\ \mathrm{pm}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bonds in \(\mathrm{O}_{3}\) have a length of \(128\ \mathrm{pm}\).

answer.text: One bond is \(148\ \mathrm{pm}\) and the other is \(121\ \mathrm{pm}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q23 - Resonance and C-O bond length in carbon dioxide

questiontext.text: The normal \(\mathrm{C=O}\) double bond length is \(121\ \mathrm{pm}\) and the \(\mathrm{C\equiv O}\) triple bond length is \(110\ \mathrm{pm}\). Why is the experimentally determined carbon–oxygen bond length in \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) equal to \(115\ \mathrm{pm}\)?

When a single Lewis structure cannot account for observed bond parameters, the molecule is described as a resonance hybrid of multiple canonical forms.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) is a resonance hybrid of \(\mathrm{: \ddot{O}=C=\ddot{O} :}\) and the two triple-bonded/single-bonded canonical forms \(\mathrm{: \ddot{O}^{-}-C\equiv O^{+}:}\) and \(\mathrm{:^{+}O\equiv C-\ddot{O}^{-}:}\). Consequently, the actual \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond length (\(115\ \mathrm{pm}\)) lies between that of \(\mathrm{C=O}\) (\(121\ \mathrm{pm}\)) and \(\mathrm{C\equiv O}\) (\(110\ \mathrm{pm}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(115\ \mathrm{pm}\) bond length in \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) arises because \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) is a resonance hybrid with partial triple-bond character.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q24 - Correct interpretation of canonical forms in resonance

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about resonance and canonical forms is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Resonance is a theoretical representation used when a single Lewis structure is inadequate; the molecule itself has one real structure called the resonance hybrid.

Step 2: Evaluation
Canonical forms have no real existence, the molecule does not spend fractions of time in different canonical forms, and there is no equilibrium (unlike keto–enol tautomerism) between them. Instead, the resonance hybrid has lower energy than any individual canonical structure, stabilizing the molecule.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Canonical forms have no real existence, and the resonance hybrid is lower in energy than any single canonical structure.

Canonical forms exist in dynamic equilibrium with each other like tautomers
The energy of the resonance hybrid is higher than that of any canonical form

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q25 - Zero dipole moment of symmetrical molecules

questiontext.text: Although the \(\mathrm{Be-F}\) and \(\mathrm{B-F}\) bonds are polar, both \(\mathrm{BeF}_{2}\) and \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) have zero net dipole moment. What is the reason for this?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The net dipole moment of a polyatomic molecule is the vector sum of its individual bond dipoles.

Step 2: Evaluation
In linear \(\mathrm{BeF}_{2}\) (\(180^{\circ}\)), the two equal \(\mathrm{Be-F}\) bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. In trigonal planar \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) (\(120^{\circ}\)), the resultant of any two \(\mathrm{B-F}\) bond dipoles is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the third, giving a net sum of zero.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The individual bond dipoles cancel each other out vectorially due to the symmetrical geometries of \(\mathrm{BeF}_{2}\) and \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q26 - Comparison of dipole moments of NH3 and NF3

questiontext.text: Why is the resultant dipole moment of \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (\(1.47\ \mathrm{D}\)) much greater than that of \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) (\(0.23\ \mathrm{D}\)), even though fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) and \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) have a trigonal pyramidal shape with one lone pair on the nitrogen atom; the net dipole moment depends on the vector sum of the lone-pair orbital dipole and the three bond dipoles.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\), the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond dipoles point toward \(\mathrm{N}\) (same direction as the lone-pair orbital dipole), so they add up to give a large net dipole moment. In \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\), the \(\mathrm{N-F}\) bond dipoles point toward \(\mathrm{F}\) (opposite to the lone-pair orbital dipole), so the lone-pair dipole partially cancels the resultant of the three \(\mathrm{N-F}\) bond dipoles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) the lone-pair orbital dipole reinforces the resultant \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond dipoles, whereas in \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) it opposes the resultant \(\mathrm{N-F}\) bond dipoles.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q27 - Fajans rules for covalent character in ionic bonds

Covalent character in an ionic bond arises from the polarisation (distortion) of the anion's electron cloud by the cation.

Smaller cation size, larger anion size, and greater charge on the cation produce the greatest covalent character.

The \((n-1)d^{n}ns^{0}\) cation is more polarising and imparts greater covalent character.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q30 - VSEPR shape and electron-pair arrangement of SF4

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q31 - VSEPR shape of ClF3

The bond angle decreases due to increasing lone-pair repulsions as the number of lone pairs increases from \(0\) to \(1\) to \(2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q35 - Zero overlap of atomic orbitals

questiontext.text: Taking the \(z\)-axis as the internuclear axis, which of the following pairs of atomic orbitals results in zero overlap?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For positive (bonding) overlap, orbitals must have the same phase (sign) and compatible symmetry/orientation along the internuclear axis. Zero overlap occurs when positive and negative phase overlaps cancel exactly.

Step 2: Evaluation
When an \(s\) orbital approaches a \(p_{x}\) (or \(p_{y}\)) orbital along the \(z\)-internuclear axis, the positive lobe of \(p_{x}\) overlaps with \(s\) to the exact same extent as the negative lobe of \(p_{x}\), resulting in zero net overlap. Similarly, \(p_{x}\) and \(p_{y}\) are mutually perpendicular and give zero overlap. By contrast, \(p_{z}-p_{z}\) and \(s-p_{z}\) give axial (\(\sigma\)) overlap, and \(p_{x}-p_{x}\) gives sidewise (\(\pi\)) overlap.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(s\) and \(p_{x}\) approaching along the \(z\)-axis result in zero overlap.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q36 - Relative strength of sigma and pi bonds

questiontext.text: Why is a sigma (\(\sigma\)) bond stronger than a pi (\(\pi\)) bond?

Step 2: Evaluation
In a \(\sigma\) bond, head-on (axial) overlapping occurs to a larger extent along the internuclear axis. In a \(\pi\) bond, sidewise overlapping occurs to a much smaller extent, making the \(\pi\) bond weaker than the \(\sigma\) bond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A \(\sigma\) bond is stronger because the extent of axial orbital overlapping is larger than that of sidewise overlapping in a \(\pi\) bond.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q37 - Essential conditions and features of hybridisation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q38 - Hybridisation and bonding in ethene

One \(sp^{2}\) hybrid orbital from each carbon overlaps axially to form an \(sp^{2}\text{-}sp^{2}\) \(\sigma\) bond, while the unhybridised \(2p\) orbitals overlap sidewise to form a \(p\text{-}p\) \(\pi\) bond. The \(\mathrm{C=C}\) bond consists of one \(sp^{2}\text{-}sp^{2}\) \(\sigma\) bond and one \(p\text{-}p\) \(\pi\) bond.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q39 - Hybridisation and bonding in ethyne

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q40 - Energy compatibility for d-orbital hybridisation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q41 - Axial versus equatorial bonds in PCl5

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q42 - Bonding versus antibonding molecular orbitals in LCAO

questiontext.text: In the linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO) method, which statement correctly distinguishes an antibonding molecular orbital (\(\sigma^{*}\)) from a bonding molecular orbital (\(\sigma\))?

Step 3: Final Conclusion
An antibonding MO has a nodal plane between the nuclei and higher energy than the combining atomic orbitals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hybridisation of \(\mathrm{Al}\) changes from \(sp^{2}\) to \(sp^{3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q52 - Hybridisation of B and N in BF3.NH3 adduct

questiontext.text: In the reaction \(\mathrm{BF}_{3} + \mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{3}\mathrm{B}\cdot\mathrm{NH}_{3}\), what happens to the hybridisation of the \(\mathrm{B}\) and \(\mathrm{N}\) atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) acts as an electron-pair acceptor (trigonal planar, \(sp^{2}\)) while \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) donates its lone pair (\(3\sigma + 1\ \mathrm{lp}\), \(sp^{3}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{F}_{3}\mathrm{B}\cdot\mathrm{NH}_{3}\), boron forms a fourth \(\sigma\) bond using its vacant \(2p\) orbital, changing its hybridisation from \(sp^{2}\) to \(sp^{3}\). Nitrogen converts its lone pair into a \(\sigma\) bond with boron, so it still has \(4\sigma\) electron pairs around it and its hybridisation remains \(sp^{3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{B}\) changes from \(sp^{2}\) to \(sp^{3}\), while \(\mathrm{N}\) remains \(sp^{3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q53 - Orbital overlap along x-internuclear axis

questiontext.text: Considering the \(x\)-axis as the internuclear axis, which of the following pairs of half-filled atomic orbitals will not form a \(\sigma\) bond?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A \(\sigma\) bond requires head-on (axial) overlap along the internuclear axis (here, the \(x\)-axis). Sidewise overlap of parallel \(p\) orbitals perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis produces a \(\pi\) bond.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(1s\) and \(1s\), \(1s\) and \(2s\), and \(1s\) and \(2p_{x}\) all overlap axially along the \(x\)-axis to form \(\sigma\) bonds.
- \(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{y}\) are oriented perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis, so they undergo sidewise overlap to form a \(\pi\) bond, not a \(\sigma\) bond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{y}\) will not form a \(\sigma\) bond when the \(x\)-axis is the internuclear axis.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q54 - Symmetry condition for LCAO molecular orbitals

questiontext.text: By convention, the \(z\)-axis is taken as the molecular axis. Why does a \(2p_{z}\) orbital of one atom combine with a \(2p_{z}\) orbital of another atom, but not with a \(2p_{x}\) or \(2p_{y}\) orbital of the same energy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the LCAO conditions, combining atomic orbitals must have comparable energies, the same symmetry about the molecular axis, and maximum overlap.

Step 2: Evaluation
Even though \(2p_{z}\), \(2p_{x}\), and \(2p_{y}\) have the same energy, \(2p_{z}\) is axially symmetric about the \(z\)-axis whereas \(2p_{x}\) and \(2p_{y}\) are perpendicular to it and have different symmetry about the molecular axis. Consequently, \(2p_{z}\) cannot combine with \(2p_{x}\) or \(2p_{y}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They do not have the same symmetry about the molecular (\(z\)) axis.

answer.text: Because \(2p_{z}\) has a much higher energy than \(2p_{x}\)
Because they do not have the same symmetry about the molecular axis

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q55 - Nature of double bond in C2 molecule

questiontext.text: According to molecular orbital theory, what is the unique feature of the double bond in the \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) (\(12\) electrons), the molecular orbital configuration is \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}(\pi 2p_{x}^{2} = \pi 2p_{y}^{2})\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The bond order is \(\frac{1}{2}(8 - 4) = 2\), and all electrons are paired (diamagnetic). Because the four bonding valence electrons occupy the two degenerate \(\pi 2p\) molecular orbitals rather than \(\sigma 2p_{z}\), the double bond in \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) consists of both \(\pi\) bonds, unlike most double bonds which consist of one \(\sigma\) and one \(\pi\) bond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The double bond in \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) consists of two \(\pi\) bonds.

answer.text: It consists of two \(\sigma\) bonds and is paramagnetic
It consists of one \(\sigma\) bond and one \(\pi\) bond with two unpaired electrons
It consists of both \(\pi\) bonds and the molecule is diamagnetic
Its bond order is \(1\) and it is unstable

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q56 - Non-existence of Be2 molecule in MOT

questiontext.text: Using molecular orbital theory, why does the \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\) molecule not exist?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Each \(\mathrm{Be}\) atom (\(Z=4\)) has \(4\) electrons, so \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\) has \(8\) electrons.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Electrons fill MOs in increasing order of energy: \(\sigma 1s,\ \sigma^{*} 1s,\ \sigma 2s,\ \sigma^{*} 2s\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\mathrm{Bond\ order} = \frac{1}{2}(N_{b} - N_{a})\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The MO configuration of \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\) is \((\sigma 1s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 1s)^{2}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}\). Thus, \(N_{b} = 4\) and \(N_{a} = 4\), giving:
\[\mathrm{Bond\ order} = \frac{1}{2}(4 - 4) = 0\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A bond order of zero indicates an unstable molecule that does not exist.

answer.text: Because it has a bond order of \(1\) and is paramagnetic
Because \(N_{b} = N_{a} = 4\), giving a bond order of \(0\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q57 - Paramagnetism of B2 due to 2s-2p mixing

questiontext.text: Why is the \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\) molecule paramagnetic according to molecular orbital theory?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\) (\(10\) electrons), \(2s\text{-}2p\) mixing places the degenerate \(\pi 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi 2p_{y}\) orbitals lower in energy than \(\sigma 2p_{z}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The MO configuration of \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\) is \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}(\pi 2p_{x}^{1} = \pi 2p_{y}^{1})\). By Hund's rule, the two highest-energy electrons singly occupy the two degenerate \(\pi 2p\) orbitals with parallel spins, making \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\) paramagnetic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{B}_{2}\) has two unpaired electrons in the degenerate \(\pi 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi 2p_{y}\) bonding orbitals.

answer.text: It has two unpaired electrons in the degenerate \(\pi 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi 2p_{y}\) orbitals
It has two unpaired electrons in the \(\pi^{*} 2p\) antibonding orbitals

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q58 - Magnetic nature of dioxygen and its ions

questiontext.text: Among the species \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}\), and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\), which one is diamagnetic?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) has \(16\) electrons; \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\) has \(15\); \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}\) has \(17\); \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\) has \(18\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A species is diamagnetic if all occupied molecular orbitals are completely paired.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\), the valence \(\pi^{*} 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi^{*} 2p_{y}\) orbitals hold \(2\) unpaired electrons.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\): \((\pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{1},\ \pi^{*} 2p_{y}^{1}) \rightarrow 2\) unpaired electrons (paramagnetic).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\): \((\pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{1},\ \pi^{*} 2p_{y}^{0}) \rightarrow 1\) unpaired electron (paramagnetic).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}\): \((\pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{2},\ \pi^{*} 2p_{y}^{1}) \rightarrow 1\) unpaired electron (paramagnetic).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\): \((\pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{2},\ \pi^{*} 2p_{y}^{2}) \rightarrow 0\) unpaired electrons (diamagnetic).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\) has all electrons paired and is diamagnetic.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q59 - Effect of ionization on bond order of N2 and O2

questiontext.text: How do the bond orders of \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) change when each molecule loses one electron to form \(\mathrm{N}_{2}^{+}\) and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) (\(14\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)) \(\rightarrow \mathrm{N}_{2}^{+}\) (\(13\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)); \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) (\(16\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)) \(\rightarrow \mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\) (\(15\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Removing an electron from a bonding MO lowers bond order; removing an electron from an antibonding MO raises bond order.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\mathrm{Bond\ order} = \frac{1}{2}(N_{b} - N_{a})\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- For \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\), the electron is removed from the bonding \(\sigma 2p_{z}\) MO: \(\mathrm{BO}(\mathrm{N}_{2}) = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 4) = 3.0 \rightarrow \mathrm{BO}(\mathrm{N}_{2}^{+}) = \frac{1}{2}(9 - 4) = 2.5\) (decreases).
- For \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\), the electron is removed from the antibonding \(\pi^{*} 2p\) MO: \(\mathrm{BO}(\mathrm{O}_{2}) = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 6) = 2.0 \rightarrow \mathrm{BO}(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}) = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 5) = 2.5\) (increases).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The bond order decreases from \(3.0\) to \(2.5\) for \(\mathrm{N}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{N}_{2}^{+}\), and increases from \(2.0\) to \(2.5\) for \(\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\).

answer.text: Decreases from \(3.0\) to \(2.5\) for \(\mathrm{N}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{N}_{2}^{+}\) and increases from \(2.0\) to \(2.5\) for \(\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q60 - Why two H3PO3 structures are not resonance canonical forms

questiontext.text: Phosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{PO}_{3}\)) can be written with one \(\mathrm{P-H}\) and two \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) groups, or with three \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) groups. Why can these two structures not be taken as canonical forms of a resonance hybrid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Canonical structures of a resonance hybrid must have the exact same positions of all atomic nuclei and differ only in the distribution of electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the two structures of \(\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{PO}_{3}\), the position of a hydrogen atom changes (attached to \(\mathrm{P}\) in one form versus attached to \(\mathrm{O}\) in the other). Because atomic nuclei occupy different positions, they are not canonical resonance forms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They cannot be canonical forms because the positions of the atomic nuclei (specifically hydrogen) are different in the two structures.

Because the two structures have different numbers of valence electrons
Because canonical forms must have identical bond orders for every bond
Because the positions of the atomic nuclei (hydrogen atoms) are different in the two structures

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q61 - Magnitude of hydrogen bonding across physical states

questiontext.text: How does the magnitude of hydrogen bonding vary with the physical state of a compound, and how does its strength compare with covalent bonds?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrogen bonding is an electrostatic attraction between \(\mathrm{H}^{\delta+}\) and a strongly electronegative atom (\(\mathrm{F}\), \(\mathrm{O}\), or \(\mathrm{N}\)); its magnitude depends on intermolecular proximity.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the solid state, molecules are closely packed in an ordered arrangement, making hydrogen bonding maximum; in the gaseous state, molecules are far apart, making hydrogen bonding minimum. Furthermore, a hydrogen bond is weaker than a covalent bond (though stronger than van der Waals forces).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hydrogen bonding is maximum in the solid state, minimum in the gaseous state, and weaker than a covalent bond.

Maximum in the gaseous state, minimum in the solid state, and stronger than a covalent bond
Equal in solid, liquid, and gaseous states, and stronger than a covalent bond
